text: Dictionaries store key-value pairs, like a real dictionary maps words to definitions.
Access values by their key name, not a number position like lists.
Since Python 3.7, dictionaries remember the exact order you inserted your keys, which is often really handy.
Use get instead of brackets if you want a default when a key is missing.
Len tells you how many key-value pairs are in the dict, three items here.
Adding a new key is as simple as assigning to it, and updating an existing key works the same way.
[sigh] Keys, values, and items give you three different views to loop over — keys alone, values alone, or both paired together.
[groan] Looping over a dictionary walks its keys by default, but items gives you the key and value together each pass.
Get with a second argument returns that default instead of crashing when the key doesn't exist.
[shush] And pop removes a key entirely, returning its value on the way out.
In the next one we take on if and else. Follow so you don't miss it.
